voiceover: Bad invitation wording, rewritten line by line. Copy, Paste, Send. Today's awkward message: the reply card. I'm Norah, Wedillybird's AI host. Four lines, and line three is sneaky. Line one. Before: RSVP whenever you can. No date means no deadline, so guests hear: no rush. After: The favor of your reply is requested by October first. Or keep it casual: Can't wait to celebrate with you! Please reply by October first. Set that date at least three weeks before the wedding. Line two. Before: Will you attend? Yes or no. There's no name line, so you can't tell who answered. After: a line for names, then accepts or regrets. Here's the part people skip: read each line out loud. Line three. Before: Plus-one welcome! That doesn't tell you who is actually coming. After: What is the name of your guest? Now the place card has a name, not a mystery seat. Winter wedding on your list? Follow. Tomorrow: ten days out and nobody has replied. Line four. Before: Let us know about food stuff. That's too vague to answer, so guests skip it. After: Please note any food allergies or dietary restrictions. One more line: Please advise us if you require special accommodations. Meal choice? Offer two or three, including a vegetarian. Guests initial one. Skipping the reply envelope? Print the web address or phone number on the card. Online, the basics come first too. A Wedillybird invitation page leads with the couple's names, then the date and venue. If you stumble reading a line, a guest will too. Save this before your invitations go to print. caption:
Wedding invitation wording examples: four reply-card lines rewritten from vague to clear. Copy the reply-by line, the name line, the guest-name line and the food and needs line.
Hosted by Norah, an AI character created by the Wedillybird team.
pinned_comment:
Copy, paste, send: the reply-card lines.
1. Deadline: "The favor of your reply is requested by [date]." Casual: "Can't wait to celebrate with you! Please reply by [date]." Set the date at least three weeks before the wedding.
2. Name line: "Name ________ accepts / regrets"
3. Guest (only when a guest is invited): "What is the name of your guest? ________"
4. Needs: "Please note any food allergies or dietary restrictions." "Please advise us if you require special accommodations." Severe allergies: "For severe allergies, please contact us at [number] so we can speak to the caterer."
Meal choice: offer two or three options, one of them vegetarian, and let guests initial one (Emily Post's example options: Filet Mignon, Poached Salmon, Vegetable Curry).
No reply envelope? Print the web address or phone number on the card.
Wording is suggested, built on guidance from Emily Post, Zola and Joy.
Norah is AI-generated. Screens shown are real Wedillybird screens (demo data).

sources.fact: Sample response-card wording: 'The favor of your reply is requested by [date]', accept(s) / regret(s) or will attend / will not attend, with a line for the guest's name; guests mark their entree choice by writing a name or initials next to the selection; if replying by phone or email, print that contact line on the card

claims_review.notes: The 'Before' lines are invented examples. 'After' lines are suggested wording built on Emily Post, Zola and Joy guidance (T32/T33/T34 suggested wording), not quotes; the 'favor of your reply' phrase follows Emily Post's sample card. T29 is medium with sources-disagree, so only the reply-by date (three weeks, Zola) is used; the mailing-window numbers are left to other videos in the series. Line three follows Joy's 'name of your plus-one' pattern (T34) rather than the 'reserved seats' wording, which another script covers; use it only when a guest is actually invited. Product: S03 over two beats (about 6 s): names, date and venue first, then the reply form; no performance or speed claim.
